It records 12 partial gang activations across 500 coordinator crashes and a 9.9-second p99 for orphan-hold release. Those are separate reported measurements: one counts partial activations, while the other describes a percentile of hold-release latency.
Does “500” refer to coordinator crashes in the report, rather than just being part of the benchmark name?
Yes. The report explicitly says the 12 partial gang activations were observed across 500 coordinator crashes. The crash count is stated independently of the name GangCrash-500.
What should I understand by a partial gang activation here?

It means part of a gang became active without the entire gang activating. That is different from finding tentative holds for only some gang members: a tentative hold is not itself an activation. The report counts 12 partial gang activations, not merely 12 incomplete sets of holds.
Can I say 12 different coordinator crashes each caused one partial activation?

The report does not make that one-to-one attribution. It gives 12 partial gang activations across 500 coordinator crashes, but it does not say how many distinct crashes were associated with those activations or whether any one crash was associated with more than one. Keep the reported units and avoid converting the count into a per-crash incidence without that information.
Would it be accurate to call the result a 2.4% failure rate?

Dividing 12 by 500 gives 2.4%, but calling it a per-crash failure rate assumes each counted activation corresponds to a different crash and that a crash is the intended denominator for that rate. The report does not establish those assumptions. The unambiguous statement is 12 partial gang activations across 500 coordinator crashes.
Does the report say whether the activations followed prepare messages or commit messages?

No breakdown is given. GangCrash-500 exercised coordinator crashes after gang prepare and commit messages, but this reported result does not attribute the 12 partial activations to either message boundary or specify their sequence.
Could I explain the 12 as the result of delayed commits?

Not from this report. It identifies the observed partial activations and the coordinator-crash count, but it does not give a cause for those activations. Assigning them to delayed commits would add an explanation that is not reported here.
Do partial gang activations mean there were conflicting resource assignments?

Not necessarily. Partial activation describes an incomplete gang becoming active; a conflicting assignment would require incompatible claims to a resource. The report gives a partial-activation count, not a conflicting-assignment count. One should not substitute one measurement for the other.
Then what does the count tell us without going beyond it?

It tells us that partial activation was observed 12 times in GangCrash-500 across its 500 coordinator crashes. It does not say which workers or gangs were involved, how long those partial activations lasted, or whether they coincided with any conflicting assignments.
How do I interpret the 9.9-second p99 orphan-hold release?

It is a percentile of the measured orphan-hold release latencies. The reported p99 is 9.9 seconds. That is not a maximum, not the release time of every hold, and not a count of how many orphan holds existed.
Does p99 mean that no orphan hold lasted longer than 9.9 seconds?

No. A p99 does not establish the maximum observed latency. Some measured releases could have taken longer; the report does not give their number or duration. It also does not state a worst-case release bound.
Can we infer how many orphan holds the percentile is based on from the 500 crashes?

No. Five hundred is the number of coordinator crashes. The report does not give the number of orphan holds measured. A crash need not be treated as exactly one hold-release observation on the basis of these figures.
Where does the release-latency clock begin in this report?

The reported figure names the metric and its p99 value, but this statement does not define its start event. It would be unwarranted to say the 9.9 seconds runs specifically from a coordinator crash, from the last prepare message, or from a worker recognizing a hold as orphaned without a stated measurement convention.
And is the endpoint definitely when another job starts using the resource?

No. The metric is orphan-hold release latency, not time to another job's start or time to a new lease's activation. The report does not provide either of those later timings. Release and reuse should remain distinct when describing the number.
How should I relate the 9.9 seconds to the ten-second tentative-hold expiry rule?

You can state both values with their own meanings, but the report alone does not show that the p99 is measured from the start of a tentative hold or that every hold followed the ten-second expiry path. A 9.9-second p99 release latency cannot, without its measurement definition and sample details, be turned into a conclusion about whether every hold met a ten-second expiry rule.
Does the report establish that crash recovery restores scheduling progress within 30 seconds?

No. It reports partial activations and a p99 for orphan-hold release. It does not give the time from stabilized connectivity to resumed scheduling progress, and releasing an orphan hold is not itself proof that a gang was subsequently placed.
Does it tell us anything about tenant fairness or starvation?

No tenant-level outcome is included. The two reported measurements concern gang activation and orphan-hold release during the coordinator-crash run, not how scheduling opportunities were distributed among tenants or whether feasible demand was starved.
Can I characterize the report as showing that gangs always activated atomically except for 12 cases?

That wording assumes a count of all gang activation opportunities and a classification of every other case that the report does not supply. It is safer to say that GangCrash-500 recorded 12 partial gang activations across 500 coordinator crashes. The statement makes no claim about how many complete activations, nonactivations, or other outcomes occurred.
Give me a concise results-only sentence.
The GangCrash-500 report records 12 partial gang activations across 500 coordinator crashes and a 9.9-second p99 orphan-hold release latency.
How can workers prevent partial gang activation after a coordinator crash while releasing orphaned holds within ten seconds?

The design has to separate two decisions: whether a gang may activate, and whether a tentative hold may be released. A worker should not activate its part of a gang merely because it received a prepare or an isolated commit message; a coordinator crash can leave other workers with a different view. Conversely, once a hold is established as orphaned, it needs a safe release path that meets the ten-second requirement. The hard part is defining a gang-wide outcome workers can trust without leaving them waiting indefinitely for the crashed coordinator.
Why isn't a valid commit at one worker enough to let that worker start?

A commit's validity and the gang's activation are distinct questions. If one worker starts while other members are still only tentatively held or do not know the outcome, that is a partial gang activation. The worker-side rule must therefore specify what establishes that activation is permitted for the gang as a whole, not simply that one worker has received information about a commit.
Would requiring every worker to receive a commit solve it?

Not by itself. Messages can arrive at different times, and a coordinator may crash between deliveries. If each worker activates immediately upon receipt, the first recipient can become active while the others have not received anything. The design needs an activation condition that accounts for that gap. It also needs to state what happens if the condition cannot be established.
Can a worker hold resources for its gang while waiting for that condition?

Yes, provided the hold is treated as tentative rather than as active gang work. That distinction lets the worker protect the resources against conflicting assignments without claiming the gang has activated. The hold must eventually be resolved: either the worker learns that the gang may activate under the defined rule, or it can establish that its hold is orphaned and release it within ten seconds.
What makes a hold orphaned if the coordinator has crashed?

The crash alone is not enough to settle it. A coordinator can crash after sending a prepare or a commit message, so lack of further messages does not establish whether a gang-wide outcome exists. An orphaned hold needs a defined meaning under the protocol: a tentative claim that can no longer participate in an authorized activation. Workers need a reliable way to determine that status before releasing resources that might otherwise still be claimed.
Is there a danger that the release rule and the activation rule disagree?

That is a central danger. One worker must not conclude that its hold is orphaned and release it while another worker can still legitimately activate the gang on the assumption that the hold remains available. The two rules must derive compatible outcomes from the same gang operation, including when a coordinator crashes between messages.
Could we simply make every tentative hold expire after ten seconds?

An expiry rule can bound tentative holds, but expiry alone does not settle the status of a possible committed gang. The specification would need to make clear when a hold's ten seconds begin, whether a commit can still validly use that hold, and what happens if commit information arrives around expiry. Otherwise the worker might release the resource while some other worker treats the gang as authorized to activate.
The question says release orphaned holds within ten seconds. Ten seconds after what?

That starting point needs to be defined. It could not safely be left to each worker's interpretation. In particular, time since the coordinator became unreachable is not necessarily time since a hold was established to be orphaned. To make “within ten seconds” testable, the design must identify the event that starts the release clock and the worker-observable event that counts as release.
If the worker cannot tell whether a commit succeeded, can it wait until it knows?

Waiting protects against an unsafe guess, but an unbounded wait would not satisfy the requirement to release orphaned holds within ten seconds. The design needs a way to resolve that uncertainty within the stated bound for holds that are orphaned. That resolution cannot simply assume that an unresponsive coordinator means no commit occurred.
Does preventing partial activation require all workers to start executing at exactly the same instant?

That is not specified by the question. It does require a meaningful definition of activation under which a coordinator crash cannot leave only part of the gang active. The design should distinguish authorization to activate, workers becoming ready, and work actually taking effect. If it calls a gang active when only some members can run, it has not addressed partial activation merely by labeling the operation atomic.
What should a worker do if it receives an activation instruction after its tentative hold has been released?

It must not treat the old hold as still available or use the late instruction alone as authority to activate. The worker has to evaluate that instruction against the defined gang outcome, hold state, and applicable lease and epoch checks. The release rule and activation rule must exclude an interpretation in which an expired orphan hold can later be used to activate only part of a gang.
Could the worker release a hold and immediately accept unrelated work?

Releasing the hold establishes only that the tentative claim has ended safely. Accepting unrelated work is a separate assignment decision and still needs valid authority and conflict checks. Keeping those decisions separate is particularly important when delayed gang messages can arrive after a coordinator crash.
Where does worker-confirmed old-epoch process termination fit?

It remains a condition before a worker activates a new lease involving an old-epoch process. That check protects the transition between epochs, but it does not alone establish that every member of a gang can activate. Likewise, confirming termination does not, by itself, determine whether a particular tentative gang hold is orphaned. The worker needs to apply those conditions without conflating them.
Would a quorum-certified commit be enough to rule out partial activation after a crash?

A quorum-certified commit can establish an authoritative gang outcome, but it does not automatically establish what every worker has learned or when each may start. If workers independently activate as soon as they see the certificate, a crash or delayed delivery may still leave a subset active. A complete answer must specify the worker-side activation condition in addition to the commit condition.
Could the coordinator be the only one to tell workers that the whole gang is ready?

Relying solely on another message from the coordinator leaves the crash case unresolved: it might fail before some workers receive that message. The design needs to state how workers reach a safe outcome when the coordinator stops participating. That does not dictate a particular replacement protocol, but coordinator failure must not make partial activation acceptable or orphaned holds permanent.
What should happen to a worker that is ready to activate while another gang member cannot be reached?

It should not equate its own readiness with gang-wide activation. The precise response depends on the activation rule, which has not been specified here. The rule must ensure that an unreachable member does not leave a subset running as though the entire gang were active, and that tentative holds which ultimately have no authorized use can be identified and released within the ten-second bound.
Is preventing partial activation the same as preventing conflicting resource assignments?

No. Two gangs might never claim the same resource, yet only some members of one gang could become active after a coordinator crash. Conversely, clearing holds to avoid partial activation must not permit conflicting assignments. This question asks for both a gang-wide activation rule and a bounded, safe release rule; each addresses a different failure mode.
How would you test the proposed answer to this question?

Exercise coordinator crashes at prepare and commit message boundaries, then observe whether any subset of a gang actually activates. Separately, measure when each hold qualifies as orphaned under the specified rule and when the worker releases it, checking the ten-second bound. Cases with delayed messages matter because they test whether a worker can release a hold while another message still appears to support activation. Those are checks to perform, not results claimed here.
What if there are no partial activations, but workers retain orphaned holds past ten seconds?

Then the activation concern would be addressed in those observations, but the hold-release requirement would not be met in the cases exceeding ten seconds. Conversely, timely release would not excuse a partial gang activation. Both outcomes have to be evaluated separately, with a precise definition of when an orphan hold's ten-second interval starts.
Can you express the core design obligation without choosing an implementation?

Workers must activate a gang only under a condition that cannot leave a subset active after a coordinator crash, and must resolve tentative holds so those established as orphaned are released within ten seconds. The activation and release rules must agree on the gang's outcome, including across delayed prepare or commit messages, and neither rule may turn uncertainty into a conflicting assignment.

I propose quorum-backed gang activation barriers and placement-feasible tenant deficit queues with aging, triggering preemption on reconnection. How do those pieces work together in the distributed scheduler?

They address different parts of the scheduling decision. A quorum-backed gang activation barrier governs when a gang may become active, so an individual worker's readiness is not mistaken for permission to activate only part of the gang. Placement-feasible tenant deficit queues with aging guide which tenant's feasible work gets an opportunity, while preserving attention to work that has waited. Triggering preemption on reconnection gives the scheduler a way to reconsider occupied resources as it resumes coordinated scheduling. The proposal still needs rules that make activation, resource assignment, and preemption safe together.
Why is the barrier described as quorum-backed rather than just a signal from the coordinator?

The backing means the authority for gang activation should not depend solely on one coordinator's unconfirmed message. If that coordinator becomes unavailable, workers need a trustworthy way to determine whether the barrier was established. “Quorum-backed” describes the source of that authority; it does not, by itself, specify when each worker may start or how a worker learns that the barrier has been satisfied.
Does quorum-backed mean only a quorum of the gang's workers needs to be ready?

Not necessarily. A quorum that backs the activation decision is conceptually different from the set of workers needed to run the gang. The proposal does not say that a subset of the gang is an acceptable activation. The barrier rule must respect the gang's placement requirements rather than treating quorum backing as permission to run only a quorum of its members.
What should the barrier prevent at the worker level?

It should prevent a worker from treating its own prepare, a locally received message, or its own readiness as sufficient for gang activation. The worker needs to know that the gang-wide activation condition has been met. Otherwise different message arrival times or a coordinator failure could leave only part of the gang active, even if the intended decision was described as atomic.
Does that mean all gang processes have to start at precisely the same instant?

The proposal does not specify simultaneous process starts. It calls for a gang activation barrier, so a complete design must define what it means for the gang to be authorized to activate and how workers enforce that condition without allowing an unacceptable partial activation. Quorum backing alone should not be equated with perfectly synchronized starts.
Can a tentative hold be released while the activation barrier is unresolved?

Only under a release rule that cannot contradict a valid gang activation outcome. A hold and an activated gang are different states. The barrier must not allow some workers to activate on the assumption that all required resources remain held while another worker has safely released its hold. This proposal names the barrier but does not specify the release rule or a release deadline.
How do the tenant deficit queues relate to placement feasibility?

A deficit queue keeps tenant scheduling opportunity in view; the placement-feasible qualification means an opportunity must be assessed against the gang's placement constraints. The scheduler cannot claim to have served a tenant simply by selecting a gang that cannot be placed. Equally, it should not use difficult placement as a standing excuse to bypass feasible demand indefinitely.
Is there one queue for each tenant?

The phrase “tenant deficit queues” indicates tenant-oriented deficit accounting, but it does not fix the queue data structure or exact number of physical queues. The important proposed behavior is that tenant opportunity is tracked while placement feasibility influences which gang can be advanced. The accounting and selection rules would need to be specified to make the fairness claim precise.
Why add aging to a deficit-based approach?

Aging brings waiting time into the scheduling decision. It is intended to guard against feasible work being repeatedly passed over when other work is easier to place or resources remain occupied. It complements tenant deficit accounting, but the proposal does not set an aging rate, a priority formula, or a waiting-time guarantee. Those details matter to any argument that feasible demand cannot starve.
Would aging make an impossible placement run eventually?

No. Waiting longer does not make a gang's placement constraints disappear. Aging can increase attention to a waiting tenant or gang, but activation still requires a feasible placement and the gang barrier still applies. If a placement can become feasible through preemption, that possibility is relevant; it is not the same as declaring an impossible placement valid.
Could aging override every other tenant as soon as a gang waits long enough?

That is not specified. Aging must interact with deficits and placement feasibility in a defined way; the proposal does not choose an override rule. The aim is to prevent indefinite neglect under feasible demand, not to assert an unlimited priority for any waiting job regardless of its constraints or other tenants' needs.
What exactly is meant by triggering preemption on reconnection?

It means reconnection initiates the preemption part of the scheduling response, so existing allocations can be reconsidered as coordinated scheduling resumes. The proposal does not specify which jobs, if any, are displaced in a particular case, nor the order or timing of individual preemptions. A trigger is not permission to create overlapping resource claims: the transition from preempted work to a new gang assignment must remain safe.
Does that mean every reconnection must terminate running jobs?

No such blanket termination rule is stated. Preemption is triggered on reconnection, but whether a particular running job must be displaced depends on the placement and scheduling decision. Treating the trigger as automatic termination of all running work would add a policy the proposal does not contain.
Why tie preemption to reconnection specifically?

Reconnection is a point at which the scheduler can reconsider allocations using a coordinated view rather than relying on a partitioned view. Triggering preemption then allows placement-feasible, aging-aware tenant choices to be considered against resources already occupied by preemptible work. It does not say preemption is sufficient to restore progress, or that unsafe assignments may be made before the old claims have ended.
Is reconnection the same event as the start of the 30-second recovery window?

Not necessarily. The recovery requirement is measured after connectivity stabilizes; a reconnection event could occur before the network is stable. The proposal triggers preemption on reconnection, while the 30-second condition concerns restoration of scheduling progress after stability. A complete recovery argument would need to relate those events without silently treating them as identical.
Suppose a tenant has an aged deficit and a gang whose constraints require resources occupied by preemptible work. What does the proposal determine?

It makes that gang relevant to the scheduling decision: the deficit and aging speak to its claim on scheduling opportunity, placement feasibility identifies the needed resources, and preemption provides a way to reconsider their current use after reconnection. It does not determine that this particular gang wins, which work is preempted, or that activation happens immediately. Any eventual placement still needs a valid, safe gang activation.
Can the deficit queue select a gang before the barrier has been satisfied?

Selection for a scheduling attempt and activation are different steps. The queue can identify a placement-feasible gang to advance, but that selection does not make the gang active. The quorum-backed activation barrier remains the condition governing activation. Conflating queue selection with activation would leave the partial-gang problem unresolved.
What if the barrier cannot be established during a partition?

Then the scheduler should not represent the gang as safely activated merely to maintain activity. The barrier is meant to constrain activation when its authoritative outcome cannot be established. The proposal does not promise uninterrupted gang activation through partitions; it must preserve assignment safety and provide a way to resume progress when connectivity stabilizes.
Could the barrier itself leave holds stuck and interfere with fairness?

Yes, unless unresolved gang attempts have a safe way to conclude and release holds that cannot be used. A fairness queue cannot place feasible demand on resources indefinitely obstructed by unresolved attempts. The proposal specifies a quorum-backed activation barrier but not the precise lifecycle of a hold, so that interaction needs definition. Releasing a hold and granting a new assignment must remain separate decisions.
How should preemption interact with the barrier?

Preemption may make resources available for a selected gang, but the gang must not activate merely because preemption has been requested. The old resource claims need to end safely, the proposed placement must satisfy its constraints, and the activation barrier must be met. Those conditions prevent preemption from becoming a shortcut to partial or conflicting activation.
Does the proposal alone guarantee no tenant starvation?

It proposes mechanisms aimed at that requirement: tenant deficits, placement awareness, aging, and preemption on reconnection. A guarantee would require precise rules showing that feasible demand cannot be postponed indefinitely, including when placements are constrained and preempted work returns to the queue. The proposal does not supply those rules or report a fairness outcome.
Does it alone establish that scheduling progress resumes within 30 seconds after connectivity stabilizes?

No. The barrier may require coordination, and the time for preemption and a safe placement is not specified here. The proposal identifies actions relevant to recovery, but it does not give an end-to-end timing bound showing that scheduling progress resumes within 30 seconds of stable connectivity.
What is the most important distinction to preserve when describing the whole proposal?

Keep authority, choice, and activation distinct. The placement-feasible tenant deficit queues with aging guide whose gang is considered; reconnection triggers preemption so occupied resources can be reconsidered; and the quorum-backed gang activation barrier governs whether the gang may actually become active. None of those steps, by itself, authorizes a conflicting assignment or makes a partial gang activation acceptable.
Can you phrase it as a proposal without claiming it has already met the scheduler's requirements?

Propose quorum-backed barriers for gang activation, placement-feasible tenant deficit queues with aging for fair selection, and preemption triggered on reconnection to reconsider occupied resources. Define their interactions so workers do not activate only part of a gang or accept conflicting assignments, then assess whether scheduling progress resumes within 30 seconds after connectivity stabilizes and feasible demand avoids starvation.

I want to make the next step concrete: implement fenced quorum gang barriers and placement-aware aging deficit queues, then test zero conflicts, starvation, and 30-second recovery under partitions. How should I frame that plan?

Frame it as implementation followed by evaluation, not as a finding. The fenced quorum gang barriers are intended to govern safe gang activation despite partitions and stale authority. The placement-aware aging deficit queues are intended to balance tenant opportunity against whether a gang can actually be placed. The tests then ask whether the implementation records zero conflicting assignments, avoids starvation under feasible demand, and restores scheduling progress within 30 seconds after connectivity stabilizes.
What does “fenced” add to a quorum gang barrier?

Quorum backing concerns the authority for a gang-wide decision. Fencing concerns whether an actor operating under stale authority can still have its instructions accepted. The implementation needs both ideas to apply at the point where a gang would become active: a purported barrier should not allow an outdated actor to activate work, and an epoch check alone should not turn an incomplete gang operation into a valid activation.
Does passing the quorum barrier mean each worker can immediately treat its part of the gang as active?

That is precisely the behavior the implementation must define carefully. It needs an activation rule under which the quorum-backed barrier cannot leave only part of a gang active when messages arrive differently or a coordinator becomes unavailable. Calling a barrier “quorum-backed” does not, by itself, settle when each worker may activate.
Should the conflict test count partial gang activation as a conflict?

Keep the observations distinct. A conflicting assignment involves incompatible accepted claims to a resource; a partial gang activation means only part of a gang became active. One need not imply the other. The plan explicitly calls for testing zero conflicts, but the barrier implementation should also make its gang-activation behavior observable rather than concealing a partial activation inside a conflict count.
How would placement-aware aging deficit queues avoid simply favoring the easiest gangs?

They need to account for tenant scheduling opportunity and waiting time while checking whether a gang's placement constraints can be satisfied. If a gang cannot currently be placed, selecting it does not constitute service. If its demand is feasible, repeatedly selecting easier work for other tenants should not make it wait indefinitely. The plan does not prescribe an aging formula or deficit update rule; those must be made precise in the implementation before starvation can be assessed meaningfully.
Does aging allow the scheduler to disregard placement constraints?

No. Aging can affect how urgently waiting work is considered, but it cannot make an invalid placement valid. “Placement-aware” remains a condition on the scheduling choice, and a selected gang still has to pass the gang-activation and assignment-safety rules.
What exactly does a starvation test need to distinguish?

It needs to distinguish feasible demand that is continually bypassed from demand that cannot satisfy its placement constraints. A wait by an unplaceable gang is not, by itself, evidence of starvation under feasible demand. The test should also look beyond a momentary selection: selecting a tenant without allowing its feasible work to progress would not resolve indefinite postponement.
Is zero starvation a numerical threshold in this plan?

The plan says to test starvation, but it does not give a numerical starvation threshold or a fixed observation duration. The underlying requirement is to prevent starvation under feasible demand. A test therefore needs a clear definition of what constitutes continued feasible demand and what observation would indicate indefinite bypass, without inventing a time limit that the plan has not set.
For recovery, when does the 30-second clock begin?

After connectivity stabilizes. It should not be silently measured from the start of a partition or from the first brief reconnection. The recovery observation is whether scheduling progress is restored within 30 seconds of that stable-connectivity point.
What should the recovery test count as progress?

It should count an actual advance in scheduling that the implementation considers valid, rather than merely a reconciliation attempt, a queue reorder, or receipt of a message. The test must keep that endpoint distinct from the start of stable connectivity. The plan specifies the 30-second limit but does not choose a more detailed progress metric, so that metric needs to be stated before results are interpreted.
Could the system pass a 30-second progress test by serving only one tenant and ignoring everyone else?

That might demonstrate recovery activity, but it would not answer the separate starvation test. The plan asks for both timely restoration of scheduling progress and avoidance of starvation under feasible demand. The observations should remain separate so an early scheduling event does not mask indefinite bypass of other feasible work.
Should the partition tests include stale actors and unfinished gang attempts?

Those are directly relevant to the zero-conflict objective. Stale authority probes whether fencing is enforced; unfinished gang attempts probe whether the barrier and resource-claim rules allow incompatible assignments or invalid activation. The plan does not prescribe a particular partition schedule or number of cases, so coverage should be described as test conditions rather than as results already obtained.
Could a system report zero conflicts merely because it refuses to schedule throughout the tests?

Yes. That is why the measurements should not be collapsed into a single pass condition. Refusing every assignment could avoid conflicts, but it would not demonstrate scheduling progress within 30 seconds after connectivity stabilizes or freedom from starvation under feasible demand.
Does the plan say preemption must occur whenever a tenant's deficit grows?

No. It specifies fenced quorum gang barriers, placement-aware aging deficit queues, and tests for the stated properties. Preemptible gang jobs make resource reallocation relevant, but this plan does not define a rule that triggers preemption at a particular deficit or for every waiting gang.
How should I keep implementation claims separate from test claims?

Use implementation language for what you intend to build: fenced quorum gang barriers and placement-aware aging deficit queues. Use evaluation language for what you intend to check: zero conflicting assignments under partitions, starvation under feasible demand, and restoration of scheduling progress within 30 seconds after connectivity stabilizes. Do not describe those test targets as observed outcomes.
What if the barrier keeps assignments safe but leaves a gang waiting through a partition?

Safety during a partition does not require every gang to keep advancing when authority cannot be established. The recovery test addresses what happens after connectivity stabilizes, and the starvation test addresses feasible demand that might otherwise be bypassed indefinitely. A wait during uncertainty should not be called a conflict, but neither should it be used to assume the recovery and fairness targets are met.
Can we evaluate the barrier and queues independently?

You can inspect their behavior separately, but the scheduler-level tests need their interaction. A queue can select feasible work without being able to activate it safely; a barrier can activate safely while the queue repeatedly neglects a tenant. The combined implementation must be assessed against all three planned tests.
Give me a concise statement of the planned work.

Implement fenced quorum gang barriers and placement-aware aging deficit queues. Test the combined scheduler under partitions for zero conflicting assignments and starvation under feasible demand, and verify whether scheduling progress resumes within 30 seconds after connectivity stabilizes. Those are planned tests, not reported results.

For the gang activation work, implement fenced, quorum-logged gang-ready certificates and worker start barriers with timeout rollback. Then retest GangCrash-500's 12 partial-activation cases. How should I describe this activity?

Describe it as an implementation and targeted retest, not as an achieved result. The work is to add fenced, quorum-logged certificates for gang readiness, enforce worker start barriers, and provide timeout rollback for attempts that do not complete. Then rerun the 12 partial-activation cases identified in GangCrash-500 to see whether those cases still produce partial gang activations. The activity does not yet report the retest outcome.
What should a gang-ready certificate mean?

It should provide verifiable evidence of a gang-wide ready state under the rules you implement, rather than merely recording that one worker is ready. The quorum-logged qualification makes that state more than a coordinator's unsupported local assertion. The implementation still has to define exactly what readiness attests to and what workers may do with the certificate; calling it gang-ready must not silently equate readiness with starting the gang.
Does quorum-logged mean only a quorum of the gang's workers must be ready?

No such interpretation is specified. The quorum concerns how the gang-ready certificate is logged and made authoritative; it is not permission to start only a subset of the gang. The worker start barrier still has to enforce the relevant gang-wide start condition.
What does fencing contribute to the certificate?

It keeps a certificate or related instruction from being treated as valid solely because it was once issued. Workers need to respect the authority boundary when considering readiness and start. A fenced certificate should not give an actor operating under stale authority a way to initiate a new start. The activity does not prescribe a certificate format or a particular fencing procedure.
If a worker sees a valid gang-ready certificate, can it start immediately?

Not simply because it sees the certificate. The proposal includes worker start barriers as a separate component. Readiness evidence and permission for a worker to start must be related by an explicit rule that does not leave only some members active if messages arrive unevenly or the coordinator fails. What the certificate permits before the barrier is satisfied needs to be defined in the implementation.
Is a start barrier just a message broadcast to all workers?

The activity does not define it as a broadcast. A message can reach one worker before another, and merely sending it does not establish how their start decisions remain coordinated. The barrier is a worker-enforced condition; the implementation needs to say what establishes that condition and what a worker does if it cannot establish it.
Does the barrier require perfectly simultaneous process starts?

The activity does not claim perfect simultaneity. Its target is the partial-activation behavior exercised by the retest cases. To evaluate it, the implementation needs an observable definition of when a gang member becomes active and a barrier rule that prevents a coordinator crash from leaving an impermissible subset active. Simply labeling starts as coordinated would not settle what actually happens at the workers.
Where does timeout rollback enter the sequence?

It provides a defined way to end an attempt when its start barrier cannot be completed within the applicable timeout. The implementation should distinguish a waiting or tentative state from an active gang, and specify what rollback reverses in the waiting state. The activity does not state the timeout duration, so it would be inaccurate to attach a numerical deadline to this rollback.
Can a worker roll back on timeout even if another worker has already started?

That is precisely the boundary the rules must settle. If one worker can validly start while another can time out and roll back the same gang attempt, the mechanism risks the partial activation it is meant to address. The start and rollback rules need to give workers compatible interpretations of the gang's outcome, including when they learn about that outcome at different times.
Is timeout rollback the same thing as releasing an orphaned hold?

They can be related, but they are not automatically identical. Rollback describes what happens to an incomplete gang-start attempt when its timeout rule applies; releasing an orphaned hold concerns removing a tentative resource claim safely. The implementation should make clear which holds rollback releases and ensure that the release cannot contradict a valid gang outcome. This activity does not provide a measured hold-release time.
Could the timeout alone certify that no gang-ready certificate exists?

Not without a rule that makes those outcomes compatible. A worker's local timer expiring does not, by itself, tell it what another participant may have logged or learned. The specification for quorum logging and timeout rollback must establish when an attempt can no longer proceed, so workers cannot both roll it back and validly start it.

Prioritize parallel worker-inventory revalidation while retaining verified-worker gating; defer repeated-failover rollout until p99 scheduling recovery falls strictly below 30 seconds.
I propose parallelizing epoch-bound worker-inventory attestations across 32 shards, admitting only verified workers and retaining quorum-backed gang barriers. How do these parts fit together?

The 32 shards provide a way to pursue worker-inventory attestation in parallel. Binding each attestation to an epoch keeps the evidence tied to the authority under which it was obtained. Admission then remains a separate decision: a worker becomes eligible for scheduling only after its relevant state is verified. Quorum-backed gang barriers remain in place so verification of individual workers is not mistaken for authorization to activate only part of a gang. This is a proposed arrangement, not a measured recovery or safety result.
What does an inventory attestation establish in this proposal?

It is intended to provide a trustworthy basis for assessing a worker’s reported state during reconciliation. The proposal does not define the attestation’s contents, how it is checked, or exactly which facts suffice for verification. Those rules would need to be explicit before an attestation could make a worker eligible for scheduling.
Why make the attestations epoch-bound?

An attestation about a worker’s state should not be treated as timeless. Binding it to an epoch makes its relevance to a scheduling-authority transition explicit: evidence associated with one epoch cannot silently serve as verification under another. The proposal does not say that every epoch change automatically invalidates every observation; it calls for a defined relationship between the attestation’s epoch and the authority under which a worker is admitted.
Would a newer epoch number, by itself, make an attestation trustworthy?

No. An epoch identifies a context for the evidence; it does not establish that the inventory was checked correctly or that the worker is verified. The worker must satisfy the verification rule before admission. Likewise, an epoch change must not be taken as proof that any relevant earlier work has ended.
What is gained by using 32 shards?

Thirty-two is the proposed number of reconciliation shards. Parallel work across them could let eligible workers be identified without requiring one serial pass over all worker inventories. The proposal does not specify the distribution of workers across shards, the concurrency limit, or a measured speedup; the number is a configuration choice stated here, not a performance result.
Does a completed shard mean every worker associated with it is verified?

Not automatically. Shard progress and worker verification must be distinguishable. Whether completion certifies every worker in a shard depends on rules that the proposal does not spell out. The admission condition remains specific: only workers that actually meet the verification rule may be scheduled.
Could the scheduler admit workers as their individual attestations are verified, even if other shards are still working?

That is consistent with the proposed separation between parallel reconciliation and verified-worker admission, provided the particular workers needed for a scheduling decision are verified. Work still in progress on an unrelated shard need not be mistaken for verification of its workers. The proposal does not require every shard to finish before any scheduling decision, nor does it license use of an unresolved worker.
What if a gang needs workers in more than one shard?

Parallelism does not relax the gang’s requirements. Every worker selected for that placement must be eligible under the verification condition, whichever shard handled its attestation. The gang must also satisfy its placement constraints and the quorum-backed activation barrier. Verification of workers in one shard does not authorize a partial gang start while needed workers in another shard remain unverified.
Could we begin a gang on the verified workers and add the others later?

That would treat a verified subset as if it were the complete gang. The proposal retains quorum-backed gang barriers precisely as a separate condition on activation. Individual worker eligibility is necessary for the proposed placement, but it is not a replacement for a gang-wide activation decision.
Is the quorum in the gang barrier the same thing as the 32 reconciliation shards?

No. Thirty-two counts the proposed shards used for parallel inventory attestation. Quorum backing describes how the gang activation barrier obtains authoritative support. A shard count is not a quorum size, and quorum backing is not permission to activate only a quorum of the workers the gang requires.
If the scheduler receives an attestation from a worker, is that worker immediately admitted?

Receipt and verification are distinct. The proposal admits only verified workers, so an attestation must meet whatever checks define verification before it can support a scheduling decision. Merely receiving a message or recording that a shard has begun work should not count as admission.
What if an attestation is delayed?

The affected worker cannot be treated as verified just because its information is expected. Other workers whose relevant states have been verified may be considered for safe placements, subject to gang-wide and placement conditions. Whether such a placement exists is not guaranteed by the proposal.
And what if the attestation arrives after the scheduling epoch has changed?

The epoch binding must be checked before the evidence is used. A late attestation cannot silently certify a worker for a different epoch simply because it finally arrived. The proposal leaves the exact treatment of late evidence to be specified, but it cannot override the verified-worker admission condition.
Could parallel attestations return inconsistent reports about one worker?

The verification rule would have to resolve any relevant inconsistency before admitting that worker. Running work in parallel is not permission to choose whichever report makes placement easiest. The proposal does not specify how overlapping attestations are assigned to shards or resolved, so it should not be described as having already settled that case.
Does retaining the gang barrier make inventory verification redundant?

No. Verification concerns whether each worker’s state can safely support a proposed assignment; the barrier concerns whether the gang as a whole may activate. A quorum-backed barrier cannot turn an unverified worker into a safe resource, and verification of every selected worker does not by itself authorize a gang start.
Does the proposal automatically protect against a stale scheduler?

Epoch binding and verified-worker admission are intended to prevent stale information from becoming scheduling authority, while the gang barrier constrains activation. But the proposal does not specify every fencing or acceptance rule. Its components should not be presented as a proof that every stale-scheduler action is rejected; the worker-side and authority checks would still need to be defined.
Could an apparently free inventory entry authorize reuse of a resource?

Not solely because it appears free. The relevant attestation must pass verification in its epoch, and the assignment still has to be valid under the resource and gang-activation rules. An inventory report is evidence to reconcile, not an independent lease or permission to ignore another claim.
What about tentative gang holds that show up in an inventory?

They must remain distinct from active, committed gang assignments and from genuinely available resources. An attestation can inform reconciliation about the hold, but verification cannot simply relabel an unresolved hold as free. Its safe resolution and any subsequent gang activation remain separate matters; this proposal does not give a new hold-release deadline.
Does admitting a verified worker mean a gang has been placed?

No. Admission says that the worker is eligible to be considered. A placement still needs the gang’s required workers, valid resource assignments, satisfaction of its placement constraints, and the quorum-backed activation barrier before it can be treated as an active gang. Counting admission alone as scheduling progress would conflate those steps.
Does this proposal choose which tenant’s feasible gang is selected?

It does not. It describes parallel attestation, verified-worker admission, and retained gang barriers. Tenant selection and avoidance of starvation under feasible demand remain scheduling-policy questions. The verification gate limits which resources may safely be used; it does not, on its own, distribute opportunities fairly.

No. The recovery requirement is to restore scheduling progress within 30 seconds after connectivity stabilizes. Parallel attestation across 32 shards may help, but the proposal provides no timing measurement for verification, gang placement, or activation. It should not be turned into a 30-second guarantee simply because the work is parallel.

Record when relevant attestations were verified, which workers were admitted when assignments took effect, and when a gang achieved a valid placement through its barrier. Then measure recovery separately from conflicting assignments or partial activations. A fast decision that uses an unverified worker would not demonstrate the proposal’s intended safe recovery, even if that particular run happened not to record a conflict. Those are suggested checks, not results reported here.

Parallelize epoch-bound worker-inventory attestations across 32 shards, admit only verified workers to scheduling, and retain quorum-backed gang barriers for activation. The proposal specifies these components without claiming a measured safety or recovery outcome.

They affect which worker state the scheduler may rely on when assigning resources, particularly around a failover. The plan does not impose a global all-workers-complete condition. But if a proposed gang needs an unverified worker, the scheduler cannot count only its verified members as a complete placement.
Why retain fenced gang barriers when we are verifying inventories?

They answer different questions. Inventory attestation concerns the state of candidate workers; a fenced gang barrier concerns authority for a gang-wide activation. Knowing that several workers are eligible does not mean their gang may start as separate pieces. Conversely, an activation barrier cannot make an unverified resource safe to assign.
What should the fencing part prevent?

It should prevent stale authority from making an activation effective merely by presenting an old instruction or view. The plan calls for fenced barriers, so the implementation needs a worker-side interpretation of which activation authority is acceptable. It does not specify a particular token format or claim that an epoch check alone resolves every incomplete gang reservation.
Could a barrier mark the gang active once only some workers are ready?

That would undermine the gang-wide condition the barrier is meant to enforce. Readiness of a subset, a partial reservation, and an authorized gang activation must remain distinct. The implementation needs to define the barrier so that an interrupted attempt does not turn into an effective partial activation or a conflicting claim.
Where do aging deficits come into the same plan?

They govern selection among tenants and waiting work once the scheduler has placement possibilities it can use safely. Deficit accounting keeps tenant opportunity in view; aging keeps waiting feasible demand from being repeatedly overlooked. Neither mechanism can waive placement constraints, worker verification, or the fenced gang barrier.
Does this plan fix a particular deficit formula or aging rate?

No. It calls for aging deficits but provides no formula, rate, credit cap, or queue ordering. Those details would have to be specified to make the fairness behavior testable. The plan’s test of feasible-tenant starvation cannot be replaced by assuming that a mechanism named ‘aging’ necessarily prevents it.
How should the scheduler treat a tenant’s gang that cannot currently be placed?

It should distinguish an unplaceable gang from one that has received service. Aging or deficit accounting should not turn an unsuccessful placement check into an allocation. At the same time, an infeasible gang should not permanently block consideration of other tenants’ feasible work. This plan does not choose the precise queue rule for those cases.
When testing conflicts, what should actually be counted?

Count incompatible resource assignments that take effect. A stale request that workers reject, an inventory discrepancy, or a tentative hold is not automatically a conflicting accepted assignment. The test should also retain enough distinction between tentative reservation and gang activation to avoid reporting one as the other.
Could the conflict test pass because the scheduler refuses all work after a failover?

A run with no accepted assignments might record no conflicts, but that would not demonstrate recovery within 30 seconds or continued opportunity for tenants with feasible demand. The three tests address different obligations. The plan should not allow a safety count alone to stand in for scheduling progress.
How do we define feasible-tenant starvation for the test?

The test needs to identify tenants with demand that can satisfy its placement constraints and then observe whether their work is continually passed over while scheduling proceeds. It should distinguish that condition from waiting because a placement is unavailable. The plan does not set a numerical tenant-wait threshold, so one should not be invented as part of the stated test target.
If a tenant is selected by the aging deficit policy but its gang never activates, has it avoided starvation?

Selection or an accounting update alone would not demonstrate that its feasible work made progress. The observation should reflect what scheduling actually accomplished, while distinguishing a valid gang activation from preparation that never completed. Otherwise queue activity could conceal continued postponement of feasible demand.
What exactly is the 30-second failover recovery test checking?

It should check the elapsed time until valid scheduling progress resumes after connectivity stabilizes in the failover scenario. Thirty seconds is the recovery condition, not a deadline for every waiting gang to start. Completing an attestation, transferring authority, or satisfying a barrier without a valid scheduling advance should not silently be counted as recovered scheduling.
If coordinator failover happens more than once, do we restart the 30-second clock each time?

The stated recovery requirement begins after connectivity stabilizes; a coordinator change is not automatically a new clock start. A test should define its observation boundaries and include the effects of failover within them rather than resetting the interval without saying so. The plan does not prescribe how many failovers to inject.
Does parallelizing attestations establish that we will meet that recovery condition?

No. It is an implementation approach intended to make verification less of a scheduling bottleneck. Whether valid scheduling progress returns within 30 seconds still depends on the completed checks, safe assignments, and gang activation in the tested conditions. The plan states a recovery test, not a measured timing result.
What if recovery is fast only because the scheduler uses an unverified worker?

That would not demonstrate the intended recovery path. A valid scheduling advance must satisfy the worker-state and fenced activation rules, not merely happen quickly. The evaluation should keep verification status visible when interpreting both the conflict count and the 30-second recovery measurement.
Do these tests establish that every possible partition and demand pattern is safe and fair?

No finite test set automatically establishes a universal guarantee. The plan is to implement the three named mechanisms and test conflicts, starvation under feasible demand, and 30-second failover recovery. Report the conditions and outcomes of those tests when available, without extending them to untested executions.

Implement parallel epoch-bound worker-inventory attestations, fenced gang barriers, and aging deficits. Test the combined scheduler for conflicting assignments, starvation of tenants with feasible demand, and restoration of valid scheduling progress within 30 seconds after connectivity stabilizes during failover. The results remain to be measured.
